svg.title: H / VPC peering alone is not an RP replacement
svg.desc: Whole-network integration is broader than service access: overlap, policy coverage, Palo insertion and capacity remain.. Blue lines show application traffic; green dashed lines show return traffic; amber dotted lines show native health checks; gray dotted lines show resource or policy references. Purple lines show policy-directed inspection. Red lines show rejected or bypass paths. See adjacent ADR option for requirements.

g.text: H1. Keep the existing passthrough NLB and remove the RP
The producer frontend cannot attach native workload backends in the other VPC, even when peered.
Peering does not change backend membership rules
No valid application path is created.
H2. Change to a supported internal TCP proxy NLB and add peering
Hypothetical only: address-overlap feasibility is UNPROVEN; eligible backend ownership and firewall permission required.
Proxy-only sources are managed Envoy, not tagged RP VMs
No Palo inspection on this shown path.
Not selected for matched peer subnet
This rejection is about forward insertion.
Peering alone does not inherit the RP-tagged regional PA
Native VM probes use Google special paths.
Healthy backends do not establish PA transit.
Capacity is coupled, not universally halved
Applicable peering-group quotas count local and direct-peer resources. Examples include subnet
Equal-limit illustration only: two standalone budgets of N can become one combined effective
budget of N. An equal allocation is N/2 each, not an enforced split.
VM-instance and alias-IP peering-group quotas are deprecated; those quotas remain per-network.
Actual limits and usage were not read.
H0: whole-VPC scope and unproven address feasibility
Actual subnet ranges and existing imported peering routes have NOT been audited. Overlap is a
potential hard blocker, not a confirmed conflict.
ALL primary and secondary private IPv4 subnet routes are exchanged across regions, including GKE
Disabling custom-route exchange does not hide conflicts; peering adds no NAT. New
Firewall denies restrict connections, not route exchange. Peering shares neither firewall policy nor
H1/H2 pattern repeats in us-central1 and the second region; no deployment is asserted.
H3. New reachability can reuse broad existing egress permissions
Hypothetical risk, not proof of deployed access. Application authentication remains a separate control.
Earlier applicable denies can still block.
0.0.0.0/0 includes private addresses, not only the
New peer destinations may already match broad
No new source allow rule is necessarily needed.
Implied ingress DENY if no earlier rule decides access.
Implied ingress ALLOW if no applicable rule decides access.
Do not assume one uniform ingress boundary
Explicit supported destination policy is required for these managed frontends. Other managed services need service-specific assessment.
Peering creates routes, not universal authorization. Whether acquired workloads gain access depends on actual topology and effective controls.
H4. A separate NSI design moves Palo enforcement to covered workload interfaces
Hypothetical interception, not a routed peering border and not automatic coverage of managed-service endpoints.
Ingress rule: actual source ranges + covered targets + apply_security_profile_group
Not a VPC route next hop.
Coverage and fallback are acceptance gates
Cover supported targets/zones and prevent earlier allow-rule bypass. Incomplete NSI configuration has a documented ALLOW fallback.
Route-based insertion is not universally impossible
Source-side PBR can steer eligible controlled VMs before subnet routes. PBR is not exchanged
and is not a generic peering-ingress hook.
Managed Envoy source applicability is not established by the documented PBR target list. A
Preserve the service boundary and match real sources
Direct peer ingress: peer workload IP ranges. PSC passthrough: producer NAT ranges. Managed
Option G retains PSC service publication; it does not require whole-network peering. Any peering +
NSI proposal is a separate redesign.
GCP third-party ingress | Reverse proxy removal | Architecture options | 2026-10-12
H / VPC peering alone is not an RP replacement
Whole-network integration is broader than service access: overlap, policy coverage, Palo insertion and capacity remain.
REJECTED AS A STANDALONE FIX / NOT A CLAIM THAT PEERING CANNOT CONNECT VPCS
